title: Sentence Similarity
statement:
Two sentences are given as word arrays, `sentence1` and `sentence2`, together with `similarPairs`, where each entry `[x, y]` declares the words `x` and `y` similar. Return `true` if the two sentences are similar and `false` if they are not.

The sentences are similar exactly when both of these hold:

- they have the same number of words;
- at every index `i`, the words `sentence1[i]` and `sentence2[i]` are similar.

Two words are similar when they are identical (the comparison is case-sensitive), or when `[a, b]` or `[b, a]` appears in `similarPairs`, so a listed pair works in both directions. Similarity does not chain: listing `a` with `b` and `b` with `c` does not make `a` and `c` similar.
constraints: Words in sentence1 and sentence2 contain only English letters (lowercase and uppercase)
Each word in similarPairs has 1 to 20 English letters (lowercase and uppercase)
All pairs in similarPairs are distinct
signature: boolean areSentencesSimilar(String[] sentence1, String[] sentence2, List<List<String>> similarPairs)
notes:
## Intuition

Only words at the same index are ever compared, and each comparison asks one question: is this exact pair listed (in either order)? Scanning `similarPairs` for every index answers it in O(m) per word, O(n·m) overall. Putting every listed pair into a hash set, once in each direction, turns each question into a single O(1) lookup. Similarity never chains, so no graph search is needed.

## Approach

1. If the sentences have different lengths, return `false` at once.
2. For each pair `[x, y]`, add the keys `x#y` and `y#x` to the set `similar`. The `#` cannot appear in a word, so keys never collide.
3. Walk the indexes `i`. Identical words `first` and `second` are always fine, so skip them.
4. Otherwise, if `first#second` is not in `similar`, return `false`.
5. If every index passed, return `true`.

## Example 1, step by step

Both sentences have 3 words. `similar` holds `great#fine`, `fine#great`, `drama#acting`, `acting#drama`, `skills#talent` and `talent#skills`.
- `i = 0`: `great` vs `fine`: `great#fine` is present.
- `i = 1`: `acting` vs `drama`: `acting#drama` is present thanks to the reversed key, even though the pair was listed as `["drama", "acting"]`.
- `i = 2`: `skills` vs `talent`: present.

Every index passes, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(m + n·L): building the set touches each of the `m` pairs once, and each of the `n` positions does one lookup on keys of length up to `L`.
- Space: O(m·L) for the stored keys.

## Pitfalls

- Store both directions; `["drama", "acting"]` must also match `acting` against `drama`.
- Do not follow chains of pairs: that is Sentence Similarity II, and here it gives wrong `true` answers.
- Check the lengths first; a shorter sentence would otherwise pass every index it has.
- Joining words without a separator can make different pairs share a key (`ab`+`c` and `a`+`bc`).

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `similar` | set of `x#y` keys for every listed pair, in both orders |
| `x`, `y` | the two words of one listed pair |
| `i` | the index being compared |
| `first`, `second` | the words at index `i` in `sentence1` and `sentence2` |
